findings.title: Google Calendar sharing path reads .data off a fetch Response
findings.body: In credential-sharing mode refreshOAuthTokens (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts) returns the raw fetch Response when CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, but this code treats the result like Google's refreshToken() return value and reads res?.data. A Response has no data property, so token is undefined and token.access_token throws. The surrounding catch (message !== invalid_grant) swallows it and returns myGoogleAuth still holding the expired token, so subsequent Google Calendar API calls fail with 401. The feature silently never refreshes Google tokens.

findings.title: HubSpot sharing path stores a raw Response as the credential key
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response when credential sharing is enabled, but here the result is used as a HubspotToken object: hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn is undefined so expiryDate becomes NaN, and the Response is passed directly to prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken } }). A Response serializes to {} in JSON, so the stored credential key is destroyed and all HubSpot calls fail. In the non-sharing path the refresh function returned a parsed HubspotToken, so the two return types are incompatible.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sharing path crashes reading .data on a Response
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response; in the non-sharing path it returns the axios response that has .data. This code then evaluates tokenInfo.data.error, so in sharing mode tokenInfo.data is undefined and the property access throws a TypeError, breaking token refresh entirely. The two branches return incompatible types and the feature does not work for Bigin.

findings.title: Zoho CRM sharing path crashes reading .data on a Response
findings.body: With credential sharing enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but this code expects the axios result and reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error. In sharing mode .data is undefined, so the property access throws a TypeError and token refresh is broken. Non-sharing returns the axios response (with .data), so the two paths are type-incompatible.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that collapse to [object Object] and strips all fields
findings.body: The schema builds keys via [z.string().toString()]. Zod does not override toString, so z.string().toString() evaluates to the literal string [object Object]; both computed keys collapse to the same name and the last one wins. The schema is effectively { access_token: z.string(), '[object Object]': z.unknown().optional() }, which is not the intended 'any numeric property is expiry' validation. Because Zod strips unknown keys by default, the parsed output contains only access_token, so in sharing mode every caller loses expiry_date/expires_in/refresh_token and ends up storing credentials with NaN expiry or missing fields, causing repeated refreshes or stalled tokens.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token' and persisted
findings.body: When the parsed response has no refresh_token (exactly the sharing case, where the sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry), this assigns the literal string 'refresh_token'. Callers such as Office365 and Zoom then write the parsed object back to the credential, overwriting the real stored refresh token with this placeholder. The next time a real refresh is attempted against the provider it fails because the stored refresh token is now the string 'refresh_token'. This silently corrupts credential data.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==
findings.body: The incoming CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET header is compared to process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET with !==. String inequality short-circuits at the first differing byte, leaking timing information about the expected secret and enabling a timing side-channel to guess it. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers). Also note the header name is looked up case-sensitively from process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME; since Node lowercases incoming header names, a non-lowercase value makes every request fail with 403.

findings.title: Malformed body or bad ciphertext returns 500 instead of 400
findings.body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) throws a ZodError on invalid input, and JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) at line 57 throws on bad ciphertext or a wrong/missing encryption key. Neither is caught, so the handler returns a 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400. This makes misconfiguration and attacker probing hard to distinguish and leaks internals. Wrap request parsing, decryption and JSON parsing and return a 400 on failure.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create race can create duplicate credentials
findings.body: The findFirst followed by create/update is not atomic. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appId) can both observe no existing credential and both insert one, producing duplicate Credential rows (the schema does not enforce uniqueness on userId+appId). Use a unique constraint with upsert, or otherwise serialize per user/app.

findings.title: Updating credentials does not reset the invalid flag
findings.body: When updating an existing credential only key is written; the invalid flag is left untouched. Services such as GoogleCalendarService mark a credential invalid: true on invalid_grant, so a credential that was previously invalidated stays invalid even after fresh synced keys are written, and the app remains disabled. Reset invalid: false in the update.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook or refresh routing
findings.body: The author states no tests were added and local tests were not run. This PR introduces a new authenticated endpoint that decrypts and writes credentials, plus a refresh-routing layer whose return type is inconsistent across callers. There is no coverage for: rejecting disabled sharing or a bad secret, decrypting and upserting credentials, and verifying that refresh flows hit the sync endpoint and still persist valid tokens. A single test exercising the sharing path would have caught the Response-vs-parsed-object mismatches in the Google/HubSpot/Zoho services.
